title: Linked Lists: Reverse a Doubly Linked List
oneLiner: Singly linked reversal flips one pointer per node; doubly linked reversal has to flip two.
keyTakeaway: A doubly linked list trades a little extra memory (one more pointer per node) for O(1) backward traversal and O(1) removal given a node reference, without needing to walk from the head to find the predecessor the way a singly linked list does. Reversing it means swapping BOTH Next and Prev at every node, not just redirecting one pointer.
explanation: Every node in a doubly linked list has two pointers instead of one: `Next` (forward, same as a singly linked list) and `Prev` (backward, the thing a singly linked list can't do in O(1) -- walking backward there means starting over from the head). To reverse the whole list, walk node by node from the head and, at EACH node, swap its Next and Prev pointers -- what used to point forward now points backward and vice versa. Keep track of the last node you touch; once the walk runs out (following the OLD Next pointer, saved before you overwrite it), that last node is the new head. Watch out for the order of operations: you have to save the old Next pointer BEFORE overwriting it, or you lose your way forward through the original list entirely.

complexity.note: Visit each node once, swapping its two pointers; no extra structure.

referenceSolutions.python:
def reverse_list(head):
    new_head = None
    node = head
    while node is not None:
        nxt = node.next          # save it before overwriting
        node.next = node.prev
        node.prev = nxt
        new_head = node          # the last node visited ends up first
        node = nxt
    return new_head
